worst.problem: Three unrelated new ideas in one step: a description meta, a viewport meta and the CSS link. The 'why' and all three hints only cover the <link>.
The expected code has <meta charset="utf-8"> and lang="en", but neither the instruction nor the hints mention them. Doctype, html, head, title and body are also too many new ideas for one first step.
It never says to create style.css. 'font-family', 'sans-serif' and 'margin' go unexplained, and the hints only cover the h1 color, not the body rule.
No step ever opens index.html in a browser, so the learner never sees their page or checks that the CSS link works.
Words like 'viewport' and 'initial-scale=1' (inside a 'line that makes it fit phone screens') would mean nothing to a first-time coder.

judgement.summary: The content steps (intro, hobbies) are well-sized and match exactly what the student asked for: their name and hobbies. The head-related steps (skeleton, link-css) ask for unexplained code that the hints never cover, and the learner is never shown how to view the page.

worst.problem: Far too big for one step: arrays, let, if, functions, addEventListener, .length and textContent all at once, with code split between two places in the file.
Uses an array before the idea is explained; the 'Lists in code' concept only comes later, in facts-list.
Four new tags with unexplained jargon ('letter set (UTF-8)', viewport, rel=stylesheet). Hint 2 names the tags but never shows the attributes a beginner can't guess.
Brings in main, div, h1, p, class and id together. Words like 'main part' and 'box' don't tell a beginner which tag to type.
Hint 3 is basically the full answer, missing only </body>, so there's nothing left to work out.

judgement.summary: The lesson builds steadily from bare HTML to styling to interactivity, with well-placed 'look at it' checkpoints and friendly personal content that matches what the student asked for. But the JavaScript jumps badly at 'faces' (many new ideas at once, arrays used before they're taught), CSS terms like flex, vh and line-height are never explained, and the face-switching extra plus the emoji standing in for a real photo drift slightly from the request.

worst.problem: Packs a variable, querySelectorAll, forEach, a function, addEventListener and classList into one step, but the only concept note covers clicks; none of the others is explained to a first-time coder.
The stylesheet link is typed before any CSS exists or is explained, while the video adds it at 724s. The later 'link-check' watch step then shows typing that the learner has already done.

The learner types class="banner", id="small-gritty" and the full relative image path here. These come before the 'paths' step explains paths and before any styling gives classes and ids a purpose; the video adds them later, at 525s, 644s and 778s.
This one step introduces a span, an id, a class, a form and two kinds of input across 9 lines. It is too many new ideas at once, and class="bold" means nothing until the 'bold' step.
The nested <div><div><span> is never explained, and the third hint gives that exact structure, leaving only the sentence to fill in.
It shares the 332-498 video clip with 'skeleton', where the video auto-generates the boilerplate, and it asks a beginner to type X-UA-Compatible/ie=edge with no meaningful explanation.

judgement.summary: The lesson follows the video's project closely, with friendly 'why' lines and a clear split between watching and typing. Its biggest weakness is front-loading the link tag and the class/id names into the HTML steps, which breaks the video's order and asks beginners to type things before they mean anything.

worst.problem: Hint 2 gives the exact full code, and hint 3 is a blanked skeleton that reveals less. The hints get weaker, not stronger, and this happens in nearly every step.
text-align: left on ul does nothing visible yet, because centering only arrives later in body-more. The learner adds a fix for a problem they have never seen.
The footer is built before the header, so the learner signs the bottom of an empty page and then has to insert content above it.
Several CSS steps (section-card, photo-style) say to insert rules between existing ones instead of adding to the end. That jumping around is confusing for a first-timer.
There is no look/refresh step during the 9 CSS steps, so the learner never sees each style change take effect. Jargon like 'sans-serif' and the '#fdf3e7' code also goes unexplained when first used.

judgement.summary: The lesson matches the request closely (name, likes, photo spot), with clear plain-language explanations and small, even steps. Its biggest weakness is hints that get weaker instead of stronger, with hint 2 giving the full answer and hint 3 a vaguer skeleton, plus an odd build order and no chance to see the CSS changes along the way.

worst.problem: Three new tags and jargon (charset, utf-8, rel, href) arrive in one step with no plain explanation of what href or rel mean.
Too many new ideas at once: header, h1, the a tag, href and links nested inside a paragraph, plus a link to contact.html, a page that doesn't exist yet.
Building the footer before the header is backwards. The learner then has to insert code above existing code, which is confusing for a first-timer.
Hex colour codes like #fff5e6 and the word serif are used without saying what they are, though the step briefly mentions 'a warm cream'.
An 11-line step whose third hint is almost the full answer. Copying could be suggested, but the hint ladder adds little.

judgement.summary: It follows the student's request closely (cakes with prices, hours, address and a contact page) and steadily builds a real two-page site with satisfying browser checkpoints. Its weakest spots are a few overloaded early steps (head-info, header) with unexplained jargon, and the odd footer-before-header order.

worst.problem: Hint 2 ('Write .card h3 { } with color #3d3030') is the entire answer, so hint 3's blanked template is weaker than hint 2. This backwards order repeats in nav-hover, banner-title, footer-css and most CSS steps.
Hint 3 starts with '….banner', which wrongly suggests something must be typed before the dot.
Uses 'px' and the two-value 'padding: 10px 30px' without explaining either. px is only explained later, in banner-title.
Hex colours like #f9f6f1 are used throughout but never explained, and 'sans-serif' is left unexplained.
The first step packs in DOCTYPE, html, head and body (seven lines and four new tags) for someone who has never coded.

judgement.summary: The lesson matches the picture very closely, building every section with sensible, well-explained HTML and CSS in a clear order. Its weakest point is the hints: hint 2 usually dictates the full answer while hint 3 is a vaguer template, so they get weaker instead of stronger, and a few terms (hex colours, px, two-value padding) are never or only belatedly explained.

worst.problem: Packs three new ideas into one step: comments, em and br. It also has the learner jump back above the h2 and then down below the bold paragraph.
Asks a beginner to type a long, unexplained meta viewport line full of jargon (charset, UTF-8, viewport, initial-scale). Its video range 162-247 overlaps the skeleton step.

Wrapping existing code is hard to picture, and the expected snippet shows an empty <header></header>. A literal-minded beginner might think the h1 should be removed. Two concepts (header and footer) are also bundled together.
The video range 288-316 cuts off the presenter adding the intro paragraph (done by 344). The watch-elements range 316-403 then starts with that coding instead of the block/inline explanation.
The attribute lang="en" is introduced without explaining what an attribute is. The expected indentation is inconsistent with later steps (e.g. h1 at 6 spaces under a 2-space body).

judgement.summary: The lesson closely follows the video's code. Its learner hints get stronger well and the third hint never gives the full answer. Some steps are crammed (em-comment-br, head-info), and the expected snippets for wrapping steps and their indentation could confuse a first-time coder.

worst.problem: Too much new at once: the style tag, CSS, selectors, curly brackets, properties and semicolons all arrive in one step, though the video splits this at 1091s and the step could be split too.

The video clip (352-720) shows the presenter bolding 'hello world!!!!!' with no

tags, so it does not match the paragraph-with-bold-name task the learner types.

Three new ideas in one step: what a tag is, the

tag, and the tag, plus multi-line nesting.
Hint 2 uses the word 'property' without ever explaining it.
Watch-step hints ('Nothing to type', 'Move on when you're ready') are filler and don't get stronger; outro also lacks its 1385-1421 video range.

judgement.summary: Its biggest strength is clear, friendly wording with short typed chunks that end in exactly the video's final code. Its biggest weakness is that the reordered HTML steps no longer match their video clips, and the CSS step crams in too many new ideas at once.

worst.problem: Asks for three meta lines, but neither the instruction nor any hint gives their values ('width=device-width, initial-scale=1.0', 'ie=edge', 'UTF-8'), so a beginner cannot produce the expected code.
Says to write a paragraph 'about Gritty's social media' but never gives the exact sentence the expected answer requires, and packs a comment, div, span, id and class into one step.
Hint 3 leaves every meta value as '…', so even the strongest hint can't get a stuck learner past this step.
class="banner", id="gritter", class="bold" and id="small-gritty" are added long before the video does, so the clips (e.g. 498-525, 525-576) show different code than the learner is typing.
Unclear whether the learner must supply a picture ('put any picture you like') or whether one already exists, since the project 'already has the same layout'.

judgement.summary: Small, well-paced steps with plain explanations of each tag and CSS property follow the video's build closely, and most third hints are good code skeletons. Some steps demand exact text or values the learner is never given (the meta tags, the Gritter sentence), and the early ids and classes make the code drift from what the clips show.
